newsitem.title: USA: Novartis buys Merck unit for $910 million.
newsitem.headline: Novartis buys Merck unit for $910 million.

text.p: Merck & Co. Inc. said on Tuesday it signed an agreement to sell its agricultural chemical business to Novartis AG of Switzerland for $910 million.
Analysts said the sale could be Merck's last big divestiture as it concentrates on its lucrative drug-making business.
The agricultural unit makes products that protect crops against mites, insects and fungi.

In December, Merck announced plans to sell its crop protection business as part of its joint venture with France's Rhone-Poulenc that combined their animal health and poultry genetics businesses into a new company, called Merial.

Analysts said Merck received a substantial price for a business some criticised as cyclical and low-profit, adding that the company was now free to grow through internal drug development, acquisitions and alliances.

"Though it's not a big deal by Merck standards, it gets the company more focused on the high-growth, high-margin business of human pharmaceuticals," said David Saks, an equity analyst with Gruntal & Co.
"They don't really have anything else left to divest," Cynthia Beach, an analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattision said.
It also could boost margins and the bottom line slightly, although most analysts said even a $910 million sale would not have much effect on Merck's massive balance sheet.

"It's a good move and helps them focus on human and animal pharmaceuticals," said Michael Binz, an analyst with Edward Jones. "It might help the bottom line a little next year, though any benefit would be negligible."
The crop protection business, based in Woodbridge, N.J., had sales of $200 million in 1996, Merck said.
Merck said the over the past four years, the operation posted annual gross profit growth of 12 percent and operating income growth of 13 percent.
While the unit had not been a drag on Merck's recent results, Saks said, "The crop protection business is cyclical, irregular pattern and low profit."
In contrast, its pharmaceutical business was growing between 15 percent and 20 percent annually with margins of between 30 percent and 40 percent, he said.
The unit dealt in niche crop protection markets, making abamectin, an insecticide marketed under the trade marks of Agri-mek and Vertimic and used on fruits and vegetables.
Avid, another of the unit's insecticides, was used on so-called "ornamentals," like roses, other flowering plants while its Zephyr insecticide was used on cotton, Merck said.
The operation also made fungicides, used after the crop is harvested, called thiabendazole and marketed as Mertect.
A Merck spokesman said Novartis made what the company considered was the best offer despite a nubmer of other "financially aggressive" bidders.
Basel, Switzerland-based Novartis is a leader in crop protection, which accounted for 73 percent of its 1996 agribusiness sales of $5.2 billion.
Novartis will offer employment to nearly all Merck crop protection employees, Merck said.
Merck's stock was 25 cents lower at $92.375 on the New York Stock Exchange in late trading. The acquisition is expected to be completed this summer.
